claim: Multiple myeloma (MM) accounts for approximately 10% of all haematologic malignancies.
source: Multiple myeloma (MM) accounts for ~10% of all haematologic malignancies.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rajkumar, 2020 in the Introduction section.

claim: The Revised International Staging System (R-ISS) was developed to stratify MM patients into stages I, II, and III.
source: The Revised International Staging System (R-ISS) was developed to stratify MM patients into stages I, II, and III (Palumbo et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Palumbo et al., 2015.

claim: R-ISS stages have distinct outcomes.
source: The Revised International Staging System (R-ISS) was developed to stratify MM patients into stages I, II, and III (Palumbo et al., 2015) with distinct outcomes (Kastritis et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kastritis et al., 2017.

claim: R-ISS stages have distinct treatment response.
source: The Revised International Staging System (R-ISS) was developed to stratify MM patients into stages I, II, and III (Palumbo et al., 2015) with distinct outcomes (Kastritis et al., 2017) and treatment response (Cho et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cho et al., 2017.

claim: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is the first human tumour virus.
source: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), the first human tumour virus (Young et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Young et al., 2016.

claim: EBV causes Burkitt, Hodgkin, and post-transplant B cell lymphomas.
source: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), the first human tumour virus (Young et al., 2016), causes Burkitt, Hodgkin, and post-transplant B cell lymphomas (Wang et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2019.

claim: EBV is associated with poor prognosis and clinical characteristics of R-ISS III in MM patients.
source: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), the first human tumour virus (Young et al., 2016), causes Burkitt, Hodgkin, and post-transplant B cell lymphomas (Wang et al., 2019), and is associated with poor prognosis and clinical characteristics of R-ISS III in MM patients (Xia et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Xia et al., 2019.

claim: The interplay between neoplastic cells and immune microenvironment cells is involved in MM progression and drug response.
source: In the bone marrow (BM) microenvironment, the interplay between neoplastic cells and immune microenvironment cell is involved in MM progression and drug response (Sperling and Anderson, 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sperling and Anderson, 2021.

claim: Myeloid cells foster cancer-promoting inflammation.
source: Myeloid cells (such as neutrophils) foster cancer-promoting inflammation, and natural killer (NK) cells and T lymphocytes mediate protective antitumour responses (Guillerey et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Guillerey et al., 2016.

claim: Natural killer (NK) cells and T lymphocytes mediate protective antitumour responses.
source: Myeloid cells (such as neutrophils) foster cancer-promoting inflammation, and natural killer (NK) cells and T lymphocytes mediate protective antitumour responses (Guillerey et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Guillerey et al., 2016.

claim: Cases of MM still remain largely incurable despite dramatic advances in therapies.
source: In spite of dramatic advances in immunomodulatory drugs (Tremblay-LeMay et al., 2018; Minnie and Hill, 2020; Nakamura et al., 2020), monoclonal antibodies (Hofmeister and Lonial, 2016), proteasome inhibitors (Ettari et al., 2018), and histone deacetylase inhibitors (Yee et al., 2016), cases of MM still remain largely incurable (Dimopoulos et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dimopoulos et al., 2015.

claim: Intratumour heterogeneity in PCs has been revealed by single-cell sequencing.
source: Focusing on PCs, intratumour heterogeneity (Ledergor et al., 2018), genome evolution (Lohr et al., 2016), and transcriptome expression signatures (Jang et al., 2019), resistance pathways and therapeutic targets in relapsed MM (Cohen et al., 2021) were revealed.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ledergor et al., 2018.

claim: Genome evolution in PCs has been revealed by single-cell sequencing.
source: Focusing on PCs, intratumour heterogeneity (Ledergor et al., 2018), genome evolution (Lohr et al., 2016), and transcriptome expression signatures (Jang et al., 2019), resistance pathways and therapeutic targets in relapsed MM (Cohen et al., 2021) were revealed.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lohr et al., 2016.

claim: Transcriptome expression signatures in PCs have been revealed by single-cell sequencing.
source: Focusing on PCs, intratumour heterogeneity (Ledergor et al., 2018), genome evolution (Lohr et al., 2016), and transcriptome expression signatures (Jang et al., 2019), resistance pathways and therapeutic targets in relapsed MM (Cohen et al., 2021) were revealed.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jang et al., 2019.

claim: Resistance pathways and therapeutic targets in relapsed MM have been revealed by single-cell sequencing.
source: Focusing on PCs, intratumour heterogeneity (Ledergor et al., 2018), genome evolution (Lohr et al., 2016), and transcriptome expression signatures (Jang et al., 2019), resistance pathways and therapeutic targets in relapsed MM (Cohen et al., 2021) were revealed.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cohen et al., 2021.

claim: Compromised microenvironment immune cells in MM have been uncovered.
source: Meanwhile, compromised microenvironment immune cells (Zavidij et al., 2020) and transcriptional alterations (Ryu et al., 2020) in MM precursor stages and extramedullary progression were recently uncovered.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zavidij et al., 2020.

claim: Transcriptional alterations in MM precursor stages and extramedullary progression were recently uncovered.
source: Meanwhile, compromised microenvironment immune cells (Zavidij et al., 2020) and transcriptional alterations (Ryu et al., 2020) in MM precursor stages and extramedullary progression were recently uncovered.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ryu et al., 2020.

claim: 11 BM samples from 9 MM patients and 2 healthy donors were subjected to single-cell transcriptome sequencing.
source: To explore the intratumoural heterogeneity of R-ISS stage-classified MM, 11 BM samples from 9 MM patients (2 R-ISS I, 2 R-ISS II, and 5 R-ISS III stage) and 2 healthy donors (healthy control) were subjected to single-cell suspension preparation and transcriptome sequencing (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1A showing the workflow.

claim: After quality filtering, 101,432 single-cell expression matrices were acquired.
source: After low-quality cell filtering, removing double cell and batch effect (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), 101,432 single-cell expression matrices were acquired.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and represents a data processing result.

claim: Dimensional reduction generated 24 clusters.
source: Subsequent dimensional reduction generated 24 clusters (Figure 1B)
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1B showing the UMAP with 24 clusters.

claim: Six clusters (4, 6, 13, 14, 18, and 22) specifically expressing high levels of CD138 were classified into PCs.
source: As is shown in Figure 1D, six clusters (4, 6, 13, 14, 18, and 22) specifically expressing high levels of CD138 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) were classified into PCs.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The identified PCs displayed obvious positive for CD38 expression.
source: The PCs also displayed obvious positive for CD38 expression.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: The identified PCs can be labeled as 'CD138+CD38+' cells.
source: Therefore, the identified PCs can be labeled as 'CD138+CD38+' cells in this study.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and is based on the expression data.

claim: All six PC clusters showed abundant expression of ribosomal proteins such as RPS2.
source: All six clusters showed abundant expression of ribosomal proteins such as RPS2,which corresponds to the antibody-producing function of PCs.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and represents data analysis results.

claim: A plasma cluster (PCC18) showed higher expression of the cytotoxic gene NKG7.
source: A plasma cluster (PCC18) showing higher expression of the cytotoxic gene NKG7 (Ng et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022) caught our attention, and was proposed as 'cytotoxic PCs'.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Ng et al., 2020 and Li et al., 2022.

claim: PCs producing granzyme B (GZMB) showed cancer cell-targeting cytotoxic activities.
source: Coincidentally, Cupi et al. reported that PCs producing granzyme B (GZMB) showed cancer cell-targeting cytotoxic activities (Cupi et al., 2014), but studies of cytotoxic PCs in MM remain limited.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cupi et al., 2014.

claim: The average proportion of PC18 (in all PCs) was 12.12% (range 0–37.01%).
source: The average proportion of PC18 (in all PCs) was 12.12% (range 0–37.01%; Figure 2B, left panel)
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: No significant difference in PC18 proportion was observed between the four groups.
source: The average proportion of PC18 (in all PCs) was 12.12% (range 0–37.01%; Figure 2B, left panel), and no significant difference was observed between the four groups (Figure 2B, right panel).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: In GSE117156 dataset, one cluster C21 exclusively expressing NKG7 corresponded to PC18.
source: In another MM single-cell dataset focusing on PC heterogeneity of symptomatic and asymptomatic myeloma (dataset GSE117156) (Ledergor et al., 2018), one cluster, C21, exclusively expressing NKG7 corresponded to PC18 in our dataset (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: In GSE117156 of all 42 samples, the NKG7+ cell proportion varied from 0% to 30.95% of all PCs, with an average percentage of 4.28%.
source: In GSE117156 of all 42 samples, the cell proportion varied from 0% to 30.95% of all PCs, with an average percentage of 4.28% (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2E.

claim: Immunofluorescence confirmed the expression of NKG7 in cytoplasm of PCs (CD138 positive) from patients with MM.
source: Next, immunofluorescence confirmed the expression of NKG7 in cytoplasm of PCs (CD138 positive) from patients with MM (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2F showing immunofluorescence images.

claim: 20 MM patients (stage I: 3 patients, stage II: 10 patients, and stage III: 7 patients) were enrolled for multiparameter flow cytometric (MFC) analysis.
source: Finally, 20 MM patients (stage I: 3 patients, stage II: 10 patients, and stage III: 7 patients) were enrolled for multiparameter flow cytometric (MFC) analysis.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: The percentage of NKG7+ PCs displayed obvious diversities among stage I, II, and III groups.
source: The results showed that the percentage of NKG7+ PCs displayed obvious diversities among stage I, II, and III groups (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The average percentage of NKG7+ population was 2.73% in stage I, 8.89% in stage II, and 0.58% in stage III.
source: The average percentage of NKG7+ population was 2.73% in stage I, 8.89% in stage II, and 0.58% in stage III (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Strong CNV signals were observed in plasma cell cluster 4 (PCC4) and 6 (PCC6), indicating their malignant features as tumour cells.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, strong CNV signals were observed in plasma cell cluster 4 (PCC4) and 6 (PCC6), indicating their malignant features as tumour cells.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3A showing CNV analysis.

claim: CNV signals were mainly located on chromosomes 1, 8 (gain/amplification) and 2, 3, and 21 (deletion).
source: Consistent with bulk genomic sequencing studies, signals were mainly located on chromosomes 1, 8 (gain/amplification) and 2, 3, and 21 (deletion) (Samur et al., 2020; Manier et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Samur et al., 2020 and Manier et al., 2017.

claim: PCs in cluster 6 (PCC6) were presumably enriched in G2/M stage.
source: Next, we analysed the cell cycle of six PC clusters, and distinguished them from other clusters, PCs in cluster 6 (PCC6) were presumably enriched in G2/M stage (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3B showing cell cycle analysis.

claim: Cell proliferation-related oncogenic markers MKI67, TOP2A, and CDK1 showed similar expression patterns over the whole cell cycle, suggesting a high proliferation potential of PCC6 in MM.
source: Consistently, cell proliferation-related oncogenic markers MKI67, TOP2A, and CDK1 also showed similar expression patterns over the whole cell cycle, suggesting a high proliferation potential of PCC6 in MM (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3B.

claim: Oxidative phosphorylation and epithelial-mesenchymal transition were the most enriched hallmark pathways in PCC4 and PCC6.
source: As shown in Figure 3D, oxidative phosphorylation and epithelial-mesenchymal transition were the most enriched hallmark pathways in PCC4 and PCC6 (Carrasco et al., 2007; Hideshima et al., 2017; Rizq et al., 2017; Azab et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3D showing GSEA results, with citations to Carrasco et al., 2007; Hideshima et al., 2017; Rizq et al., 2017; Azab et al., 2012.

claim: Most genes with high specificity in PCC6 showed elevated prognostic z-scores, such as GGH (z-score=6.1), GINS2 (z-score=4.5), PRKDC (z-score=6.1), MCM3 (z-score=4.4), SHCBP1 (z-score=4.7), CHEK1 (z-score=3.9), and PHF19 (z-score=5.5).
source: The results showed that most genes with high specificity in PCC6 also showed elevated prognostic z-scores, such as GGH (z-score=6.1), GINS2 (z-score=4.5), PRKDC (z-score=6.1), MCM3 (z-score=4.4), SHCBP1 (z-score=4.7), CHEK1 (z-score=3.9), and PHF19 (z-score=5.5) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3E showing PRECOG analysis.

claim: 75 significantly up-regulated genes in the MM (UGM) dataset of GSE6477 were discovered compared with normal samples.
source: Next, we discovered 75 significantly up-regulated genes in the MM (UGM) dataset of GSE6477 compared with normal samples (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: 20 genes were identified by comparing specific genes in PCC6 with 75 UGMs.
source: The specific genes (cluster specificity >0.6) in PCC6 were compared with 75 UGMs, and 20 genes were identified (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4C.

claim: Four genes showed good performance as unfavourable markers: HINT1 (HR=1.9, 95% CI=1.2–2.9, p-value=0.005496), TIMM13 (HR=1.6, 95% CI=1–2.5, p-value=0.03971), SIGMAR1 (HR=1.6, 95% CI=1–2.5, p-value=0.0493), and RRM2 (HR=2.3, 95% CI=1.4–3.6, p-value=0.000402).
source: Four genes showed good performance as unfavourable markers, with hazard ratio (HR) for histidine triad nucleotide binding protein 1 (HINT1) of 1.9 (95% CI=1.2–2.9, p-value = 0.005496), translocase of inner mitochondrial membrane 13 (TIMM13) of 1.6 (95% CI=1–2.5, p-value = 0.03971), sigma non-opioid intracellular receptor 1 (SIGMAR1) of 1.6 (95% CI=1–2.5, p-value = 0.0493) and ribonucleotide reductase regulatory subunit (RRM2) of 2.3 (95% CI=1.4–3.6, p-value = 0.000402) (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4F showing survival analysis.

claim: Significantly increased expression of RRM2 was observed in clinical MM R-ISS III samples.
source: Consistently, significantly increased expression of RRM2 was observed in both clinical MM R-ISS III samples (Figure 4G)
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4G showing qRT-PCR results.

claim: Significantly increased expression of RRM2 was observed in MM cell lines (MM.1S and U266).
source: Consistently, significantly increased expression of RRM2 was observed in both clinical MM R-ISS III samples (Figure 4G) and both MM cell lines (MM.1S and U266) (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4H showing qRT-PCR results.

claim: RRM2 silencing reduced the proliferation of U266 cells.
source: RRM2 silencing reduced the proliferation of U266 cells (Figure 4I)
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4I showing proliferation assay results.

claim: RRM2 silencing induced cell cycle G1 phase arrest.
source: RRM2 silencing reduced the proliferation of U266 cells (Figure 4I), and induced cell cycle G1 phase arrest (Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4J showing cell cycle analysis.

claim: HINT1 silencing reduced the proliferation of U266 cells.
source: RRM2 and HINT1 silencing reduced the proliferation of U266 cells, respectively (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4I.

claim: RRM2 specifically upregulated in proliferating PC serves as an oncogene in MM.
source: The above results shows that RRM2 specifically unregulated in proliferating PC serve as an oncogene in MM.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and is based on the experimental data presented.

claim: A total of 351 DEGs were acquired in PCC6 by comparing R-ISS stages I and III.
source: Finally, we identified the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) with fold change ≥2 or ≤0.5 and adjusted p-value <0.05 in PCC6 by comparing R-ISS stages I and III. A total of 351 DEGs were acquired and are shown in Supplementary file 1.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: Seven functional gene modules were identified in PCC6: ribosome, protein processing in endoplasmic reticulum, oxidative phosphorylation, proteasome, and EBV infection.
source: As shown in Figure 5, seven functional gene modules were identified: (a) ribosome, (b) protein processing in endoplasmic reticulum, (c) oxidative phosphorylation, (d) proteasome, and (e) EBV infection.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5 showing functional network analysis.

claim: 18 genes involved in EBV infection were identified in PCC6.
source: Intriguingly, 18 genes involved in EBV infection attracted our attention.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: Significantly elevated expression of MKI67 and PCNA was observed in EBV-positive (EBV+) MM patients compared with EBV-negative (EBV-) MM patients.
source: Indeed, significantly elevated expression of MKI67 and PCNA was observed in EBV-positive (EBV+) MM patients compared with EBV-negative (EBV-) MM patients (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5B and 5C showing expression analysis.

claim: Alsterpaullone, orlistat, moxonidine, nalidixic acid, and LY-294002 were proposed as C10-targeting pharmaceuticals in MM.
source: Finally, potential therapeutic drugs were analysed based on pathways in PCC6, and alsterpaullone (cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor) (Watanabe et al., 2020), orlistat (anti-obesity drug) (Yang et al., 2010), moxonidine (a selective imidazoline/alpha2 adrenergic receptor agonist) (Molderings et al., 2003), nalidixic acid (topoisomerase II inhibitors) (Nyce, 1989), and LY-294002 (PI3K/AKT inhibitor) (Chen et al., 2018) were proposed as C10-targeting pharmaceuticals in MM (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5D, with citations to Watanabe et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2010; Molderings et al., 2003; Nyce, 1989; Chen et al., 2018.

claim: Re-clustering of T cells generated 21 clusters.
source: First, re-clustering of T cells generated 21 clusters (Figure 6A)
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 6A.

claim: T cell clusters consist of CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, NK cells, and NKT cells.

source: In T4 CD8+ T cells, 12 gene modules with distinct expression patterns were generated, and module 7 (stable expression in healthy controls I-II and dramatic increases in stage III) and module 11 (gradually decreased expression with R-ISS stage) were chosen for subsequent analysis (Figure 7A).

claim: Genes in T4 module 7 were functionally related to haemopoiesis.
source: Genes in module 7 were functionally related to haemopoiesis, and genes in module 11 were involved in T-helper 1 cell lineage commitment (Figure 7C).

claim: Genes in T4 module 11 were involved in T-helper 1 cell lineage commitment.
source: Genes in module 7 were functionally related to haemopoiesis, and genes in module 11 were involved in T-helper 1 cell lineage commitment (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 7C showing functional network analysis.

claim: Genes in T6 module 3 were involved in regulation of megakaryocyte differentiation and regulation of myeloid cell differentiation.

claim: Genes in T6 module 7 were involved in leukocyte activation involved in the immune response.
